sections.skill: Use a rubric for human review and look for failures

questions.domain: Work: measuring how well AI works
questions.prompt: What is a rubric?

choices.text: A single overall impression of whether an answer feels good or bad to the reviewer
A list of criteria with levels for scoring

questions.correct_answer: A list of criteria with levels for scoring
questions.intro: Some outputs, such as summaries, letters or explanations, cannot be scored as simply right or wrong. Use a RUBRIC: a short list of criteria with levels, such as ACCURATE (no false claims), COMPLETE (covers the key points), CLEAR (easy to follow) and APPROPRIATE (right tone and length), each scored 0 to 2. Reviewers apply the same rubric to every output. And be wary of DEMONSTRATIONS: a demo shows chosen examples that work. Good evaluation looks for FAILURES on purpose, using hard and unusual cases.

sections.skill: Score an output with a rubric

questions.domain: Work: measuring how well AI works
questions.prompt: The note names the wrong gift. What is the Accurate score?

choices.text: 2, since naming a gift at all shows that the note is generally accurate

questions.intro: To score with a rubric: (1) read the output once fully. (2) For each criterion, decide the level, 0 (not met), 1 (partly met) or 2 (fully met), and write a short reason. (3) Add the scores. Example criteria for a thank-you note: Accurate (names the right gift), Warm (friendly tone), Brief (under 80 words). A note naming the wrong gift, friendly, 60 words: Accurate 0, Warm 2, Brief 2, total 4 of 6.

sections.title: Apply it

questions.domain: Work: measuring how well AI works
questions.prompt: Why have two reviewers score the same outputs?

choices.text: To make the review take twice as long, which always improves the final results

questions.intro: Rubrics work better when criteria are specific ("names the deadline and the fee") rather than vague ("good quality"). Two reviewers scoring the same outputs and comparing results reveals unclear criteria; if they disagree often, refine the rubric. Tired reviewers become less careful and less consistent, sometimes more lenient and sometimes harsher, so keep review sessions short. Record examples of each score level so new reviewers can calibrate.
